traveler: Lucy Parsons (born Lucia; Gonzalez, Carter, Diaz, Hull)
title: More Dangerous Than a Thousand Rioters: Waco to Haymarket to the Avondale Fire
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: Virginia to Waco: the Name She Did Not Keep

stops.name: Virginia, born to Charlotte on the Taliaferro place
stops.date_confidence: Birth year and Virginia birthplace per Jacqueline Jones, Goddess of Anarchy, and the Texas State Historical Association [A]; Taliaferro as likely father is Jones's finding [A as her conclusion]. Parsons's own lifelong counter-account, that she was born in Texas of Mexican and Native parentage and never enslaved, is [A] as her testimony and irreconcilable with the documentary record; the contradiction is left standing. Her death certificate gives 1859; libcom's entry heading gives 1853. Month and day unknown, defaulted to 01-01. The pin is the geographic centre of Virginia: no county is named in any source reachable this session.
stops.campa: A daughter is born to an enslaved woman named Charlotte on land held by Thomas J. Taliaferro, and the child is called Lucia. The historians who work the records give the year as 1851 and the place as Virginia, and name Taliaferro himself as the likely father. Lucy Parsons will spend sixty years denying every word of it, telling reporters and comrades alike that she was born in Texas of Mexican and Native parentage and was never anybody's property. Her own death certificate will give 1859. The record and the woman do not agree, and neither of them ever backs down.
suggested_refs: Jacqueline Jones, Goddess of Anarchy: The Life and Times of Lucy Parsons, American Radical (2017)
sources: Texas State Historical Association, Handbook of Texas, 'Parsons, Lucy'
Jacqueline Jones, Goddess of Anarchy (2017), via Princeton African American Studies / WBEZ

stops.name: McLennan County, Texas, driven west ahead of the armies
stops.date_confidence: Attested by the Texas State Historical Association [A], which dates the forced removal to 1863. Month and day unknown, defaulted to 01-01. The coordinate is Waco, the county seat and the family's subsequent locus, not a route point.
stops.campa: Near the end of the war Taliaferro empties his plantation and marches the people he owns west, out of the reach of the Union armies, into McLennan County in Texas. Charlotte walks it with her children. The distance is most of a thousand miles and the direction is the one slavery takes when it is losing: away from the front, deeper into cotton country, hunting a jurisdiction where the old law still holds. It holds for two more years. The girl who arrives in Texas on that march will spend her life saying she was born there.
suggested_refs: Slaveholder refugeeing into Texas, 1862-1865, and the McLennan County cotton belt
sources: Texas State Historical Association, Handbook of Texas, 'Parsons, Lucy'

stops.name: Waco, freedom, the needle, and the school for freed children
stops.date_confidence: Emancipation, the move into Waco, the seamstress and domestic work, and the school for freed children are all attested by the Texas State Historical Association [A]. Month and day unknown, defaulted to 01-01.
stops.campa: Freedom comes and Charlotte moves what is left of the family into Waco. Lucia grows up there sewing: a seamstress and a domestic servant in white households, and for a while a pupil at one of the schools opened for freed children. She learns to read, and to write well enough that police chiefs will later work to keep her off a platform. Waco in these years is a Reconstruction town, garrisoned, contested, filling with freedpeople and with the men who mean to put them back. She is fourteen, or she is six, depending on which birth year the reader takes.
suggested_refs: Freedmen's Bureau schools in McLennan County, Texas, 1866-1870
sources: Texas State Historical Association, Handbook of Texas, 'Parsons, Lucy'

stops.name: Hill County, Oliver Benton and the child in the census
stops.date_confidence: The union with Oliver Benton (1868) and the 1870 census entry naming an infant son, Champ, are attested by the Texas State Historical Association [A]. Benton's later claim that Lucia was his common-law wife and left him for Albert Parsons is [R]: it survives as an interview recollection, and historians disagree over how much weight it carries (AAIHS, 'Searching for Lucy Parsons: A Racial Riddle'). The Hill County pin is the Gathings plantation locality, where Benton had been held; Lucia herself is recorded in Waco. Month and day unknown, defaulted to 01-01.
stops.campa: She is living with Oliver Benton, a freedman who had been held on James J. Gathings's place in Hill County, and in 1870 the census taker writes her down in Waco with her mother, her brothers, and an infant son. The child is recorded as Champ. Nothing further is known about him: not where he went, not whether he lived. Benton will tell an interviewer decades later that Lucia had been his common-law wife and that she left him for a white man. She never mentions any of it again, in print or on a platform, for the rest of her life.
suggested_refs: 1870 U.S. federal census, McLennan County, Texas
Oliver Benton's interview testimony, discussed in AAIHS, 'Searching for Lucy Parsons: A Racial Riddle'
sources: Texas State Historical Association, Handbook of Texas, 'Parsons, Lucy'
AAIHS, 'Searching for Lucy Parsons: A Racial Riddle'

stops.name: Waco, Albert Parsons and the marriage no clerk recorded
stops.date_confidence: The Texas State Historical Association gives September 1872 at Waco [A]; the Dictionary of American Biography gives 10 June 1871, and other accounts give 1872 at Austin. No marriage record has ever been found, which is consistent with Texas's anti-miscegenation statute of 1858 being in force at the time. The site is unresolved: Waco is the named site in the strongest source and is used for the pin here, with Austin recorded as the alternate. Day unknown, defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: Albert Parsons comes through the county as a travelling correspondent: a former Confederate soldier, seventeen when he enlisted, now a Radical Republican registering Black voters and being shot at for it. He is twenty-three. They marry in September 1872 and no clerk in Texas records it, because the state has forbidden the thing they are doing. Within a year the Democrats have taken the statehouse back, the Klan is riding, and the marriage is a standing provocation in a town of eight thousand. They leave Texas and do not return.
suggested_refs: Texas anti-miscegenation statute of 1858, in force at the date of the ceremony
sources: Texas State Historical Association, Handbook of Texas, 'Parsons, Lucy'
Women & the American Story (New-York Historical Society)

segments.name: Chicago, the Tenement and the Needle

stops.name: Chicago, arrival in the winter city
stops.date_confidence: Arrival in Chicago in late 1873, and the political reason for leaving Texas, attested by the Texas State Historical Association and Wikipedia [A]. December is the month given in the IWW archive biography. Day unknown, defaulted to 01. The coordinate is the canonical Chicago pin used across this corpus (State and Madison), not a residence.
stops.campa: They arrive in December, in the third winter after the fire, into a city rebuilding itself at speed on cheap immigrant labour and into the worst depression the country has yet had. Albert finds work as a compositor and Lucy takes in sewing. Neither of them is anything yet but poor. The Chicago they enter is German and Bohemian and Irish in the wards where they can afford to live. Apart from the lecture tours, she will spend the next sixty-eight years inside its limits.
suggested_refs: Chicago in the Panic of 1873 and the rebuilding after the 1871 fire
sources: Texas State Historical Association, Handbook of Texas, 'Parsons, Lucy'
IWW archive, 'Lucy Parsons: Woman of Will'

stops.name: Larrabee Street and North Avenue, the tenement
stops.date_confidence: Tenement residence on the North Side around Larrabee Street and North Avenue, Lucy's seamstress work, Albert's printing work, and her joining the Social Democratic Workingmen's Party are attested [A] by Wikipedia and the IWW archive biography, dated to 1874. Month and day unknown, defaulted to 01-01. That the meetings were conducted partly in German is [R], inferred from the ward's population and the party's Chicago composition.
stops.campa: The tenement district around Larrabee Street and North Avenue takes them in. Lucy joins the Social Democratic Workingmen's Party, which is what a Texas seamstress does in this neighbourhood when she wants to know why the rent keeps rising and the wages do not. The meetings are conducted partly in German. She learns the vocabulary of the thing before she holds any position in it, and she learns it in rooms where nobody asks her what she is. Then she walks home to the piecework and the rent.
suggested_refs: The Social Democratic Workingmen's Party of North America, Chicago sections, 1874-1876
sources: IWW archive, 'Lucy Parsons: Woman of Will'

stops.name: Chicago, the great strike of 1877
stops.date_confidence: Albert's address to a crowd of some 25,000, his firing and blacklisting, and Lucy's own dating of her politics to this strike are attested [A] by the Texas State Historical Association and by her autobiographical statement. The Chicago death toll of roughly thirty is [A] from the general historiography of the 1877 strike but is not given in the pool sources. The exact site of Albert's speech is not attested in any source reachable this session; the canonical Chicago pin is used as a placeholder. The date is the peak of the Chicago disturbances.
stops.campa: The railroad strike reaches Chicago in July and Albert speaks to a crowd of twenty-five thousand. He is fired the next morning and blacklisted out of the printing trade for good; the police kill some thirty people in the streets of the city that week. Lucy watches a general strike assemble itself out of nothing in four days, and she watches the state answer it with rifles. She will date her own politics from this month, and from no earlier one, for the rest of her life.
stops.quote: It was during the great railroad strike of 1877 that I first became interested in what is known as the 'Labor Question'.
stops.quote_source: Lucy Parsons, autobiographical statement, quoted in Keith Rosenthal, 'Lucy Parsons: More Dangerous Than a Thousand Rioters'
suggested_refs: The Great Railroad Strike of 1877 in Chicago and the Battle of the Viaduct
sources: Texas State Historical Association, Handbook of Texas, 'Parsons, Lucy'
Keith Rosenthal, 'Lucy Parsons: More Dangerous Than a Thousand Rioters' (The Anarchist Library)

stops.name: Mohawk Street, Parsons & Co.
stops.date_confidence: The shop at 306 Mohawk Street, opened after Albert's blacklisting, is attested [A] by Wikipedia and the IWW archive biography; month and day unknown, defaulted to 10-01 to place it after the July strike. That 306 Mohawk is the pre-1909 number for 1908 North Mohawk, the address of the 1997 city marker, is attested [A]. The two research lenses supplied conflicting coordinates for the same building (41.911,-87.642 and 41.9147,-87.6423); both sit south of 1908 North Mohawk, so the corrected coordinate is used here for both the shop and the later marker.
stops.campa: With Albert unemployable at his trade, Lucy opens a dress and clothing shop at 306 Mohawk Street and the household lives on her needle. Parsons & Co. is a business and it is also the household's politics: the money from the fittings pays for the pamphlets. She will keep taking in sewing for another fifty years, through everything that follows. The city renumbers the street later; the address becomes 1908 North Mohawk, and a marker goes up on it in 1997.
suggested_refs: The 1997 City of Chicago historical marker at 1908 North Mohawk Street, Old Town
sources: IWW archive, 'Lucy Parsons: Woman of Will'

stops.name: The lakefront, Sunday crowds and the Working Women's Union
stops.date_confidence: The Sunday open-air crowds of 1,000 to 5,000 on the lakefront are attested [A] by Wikipedia and the IWW archive biography, undated beyond the late 1870s and 1880s. The Working Women's Union No. 1 of Chicago was organized in 1877 under Alzina Stevens; Parsons's involvement alongside Stevens, Elizabeth Rodgers, Elizabeth Morgan and Lizzie Swank is placed before 1881 [A], correcting a research entry that had wrongly dated her co-founding to 1885. Month and day chosen only to order the segment.
stops.campa: On Sunday afternoons the Parsonses speak on the open ground by the lake, to crowds that run from one thousand to five thousand depending on the weather and the season of unemployment. Lucy has by now come into the Working Women's Union alongside Alzina Stevens, Elizabeth Rodgers and Lizzie Swank, to carry the eight-hour demand into trades no union will go near: seamstresses, domestics, women paid by the piece. She argues there, as she will argue for sixty years, that a woman's dependence is first of all economic and that nothing else moves until that does.
stops.quote: I hold ... that the economic is the first issue to be settled, that it is woman's economical dependence which makes her enslavement possible
stops.quote_source: Lucy Parsons, quoted in Keith Rosenthal, 'Lucy Parsons: More Dangerous Than a Thousand Rioters' (The Anarchist Library)
suggested_refs: Working Women's Union No. 1 of Chicago, organized 1877
sources: IWW archive, 'Lucy Parsons: Woman of Will'

segments.name: The Alarm and the Eight-Hour Day

stops.name: Chicago, Johann Most and the American Group of the IWPA
stops.date_confidence: Lucy's meeting with Johann Most in 1883 and Albert's part in founding the American Group of the International Working People's Association in November 1883 are attested [A] by Wikipedia. The descent of the IWPA from the anarchist wing of the First International, after the Hague split of 1872 between Marx's General Council and Bakunin's followers, is [R]: an organizational lineage attested in the general historiography rather than in any statement by Parsons herself. Day unknown, defaulted to 01. Coordinate is the canonical Chicago pin; the American Group had no single fixed hall.
stops.campa: The German insurrectionist Johann Most reaches Chicago and the local movement turns. In November Albert helps found the American Group, the English-speaking wing of the International Working People's Association, the body the anarchists built after the split with Karl Marx's General Council at The Hague put Mikhail Bakunin's followers outside the First International. Lucy is in it from the start. The Chicago anarchists are not a reading circle. They arm and they drill, and they print the fact in their own newspapers rather than deny it.
suggested_refs: The Pittsburgh Manifesto of the International Working People's Association (1883)

stops.name: The Alarm, Fifth Avenue: To Tramps
stops.date_confidence: 'To tramps, the unemployed, the disinherited and miserable' ran in The Alarm on 4 October 1884 and sold over 10,000 copies as a pamphlet between May and November 1885 [A]. 'Dynamite! The only voice the oppressors of the people can understand' was published in the Denver Labor Enquirer in 1885, not in The Alarm and not in 1884, correcting a research entry that had merged the two. The coordinate is the Arbeiter-Zeitung and Alarm office at 107 Fifth Avenue (now North Wells Street); the address is standard in the Haymarket literature but is not printed in either Wikipedia entry consulted, so the pin carries moderate confidence.
stops.campa: Albert edits The Alarm out of the offices on Fifth Avenue and Lucy writes for it. In the issue of the fourth of October she addresses the thirty-five thousand unemployed men then walking the streets of Chicago, and tells them to learn the use of explosives. The piece sells over ten thousand copies as a pamphlet in the following year, and the year after that she puts the argument under a one-word headline in a Denver paper. She is thirty-three and keeps a dress shop on the North Side.
stops.quote: A word to the 35,000 now tramping the streets of this great city, with hands in pockets, gazing listlessly about you at the evidence of wealth and pleasure of which you own no part
stops.quote_source: Lucy Parsons, 'To Tramps,' The Alarm, 4 October 1884 (text via The Anarchist Library)
suggested_refs: Lucy Parsons, 'To Tramps' (1884), full text at The Anarchist Library
Lucy Parsons, 'Dynamite! The Only Voice the Oppressors of the People Can Understand', Denver Labor Enquirer (1885)

stops.name: The Board of Trade, the march on the banquet
stops.date_confidence: Attested [A] by Wikipedia: Parsons and Lizzie Holmes led an IWPA march protesting the banquet at the new Board of Trade Building on 28 April 1885. The black flag at the head of the column and the police turning the march before the doors are [R], standard in the Haymarket literature but not in the pool sources.
stops.campa: The Board of Trade opens its new building at LaSalle and Jackson with a banquet, and Lucy and Lizzie Holmes lead an International Working People's Association column up to the doors of it, black flag at the head. The police turn the march before it reaches the entrance, and the banquet goes on upstairs. What the marchers meant to do if they had got inside is not recorded; the police did not wait to find out. It is April of 1885, thirteen months before the Haymarket.
suggested_refs: The 1885 Chicago Board of Trade Building, W. W. Boyington, at LaSalle and Jackson

stops.name: Michigan Avenue, eighty thousand for eight hours
stops.date_confidence: Attested [A] by Wikipedia: Parsons led a demonstration of roughly 80,000 down Michigan Avenue on 1 May 1886. That the children walked with their parents is [R], from the IWW archive biography. National strike participation figures are from the general historiography of the eight-hour movement.
stops.campa: Eighty thousand workers come down Michigan Avenue on the first of May for the eight-hour day, and Lucy and Albert walk at the head of them with their two children. Chicago is the centre of the national strike; some three hundred and forty thousand are out across the country by nightfall. Nobody is killed and nothing is burned, and for one afternoon the movement can be counted from the sidewalks. Two days later the police open fire at the McCormick works.
suggested_refs: The national eight-hour strike of 1 May 1886

stops.name: The McCormick works, Western and Blue Island
stops.date_confidence: Police firing on strikers at the McCormick Harvesting Machine Works on 3 May 1886 is attested [A]. Casualties: Wikipedia gives two McCormick workers killed, with some newspaper accounts claiming six; a research entry saying 'killing several' overstated it. The coordinate is corrected to the Western and Blue Island intersection named by the Illinois Labor History Society; the lens's original 41.8524,-87.6763 lay roughly 800 m ESE.
stops.campa: Strikers and locked-out men are gathered outside the McCormick Harvesting Machine Works at Western and Blue Island when the police fire into them. Two workers are killed; some papers put the figure at six. August Spies, who has been speaking to the crowd, goes back to the Arbeiter-Zeitung office and writes the circular calling a protest meeting for the following night at the Haymarket. It is printed in German and English, and one line of the German setting, which Spies did not authorize, tells the workingmen to arm.
suggested_refs: The 'Revenge' circular of 3 May 1886, printed at the Arbeiter-Zeitung office
sources: Illinois RBML, 'A Woman's Place in Anarchy'

stops.name: Haymarket Square, Desplaines Street
stops.date_confidence: Attested [A]. The sequence is corrected here: the bomb was thrown as the police advanced to disperse the meeting, and the police then opened fire, not the reverse as one research entry had it. Casualties per Wikipedia and the Illinois Labor History Society: seven police officers and at least four workers killed, only Mathias Degan dying directly from the bomb, with Paul Avrich concluding most police deaths came from police gunfire. Mayor Harrison's attendance and departure are [A]. Parsons's meeting for the striking sewing women on the same day is [A] per Wikipedia.
stops.campa: The meeting on Desplaines Street is small and orderly and it rains. Lucy is there with Albert and the children; the mayor comes, listens, and goes home telling the police captain nothing is needed. When the police advance anyway to disperse the last speaker, someone throws a bomb, and the police open fire. Seven officers die, and at least four workers; the historian Paul Avrich concludes most of the police deaths came from police guns. Earlier that same day Lucy had held a meeting for the striking sewing women, and that is what she had gone out to do.
suggested_refs: Paul Avrich, The Haymarket Tragedy (1984)
The Haymarket Memorial at Desplaines and Randolph, Chicago

stops.name: Zepf's Hall, out of the rain
stops.date_confidence: Parsons's presence at or near Zepf's Hall after leaving the wagon is [R], from the IWW archive biography and standard in the Haymarket literature; no primary deposition is cited in the sources reachable this session. Albert's flight from Chicago and voluntary return to the courtroom on 21 June 1886 are [A]. Lucy's repeated brief detentions over the following six months are [A] per Wikipedia and the IWW archive.
stops.campa: Before the bomb the Parsonses have already left the wagon and gone into Zepf's Hall on the corner, out of the rain, with the children. The explosion and the volleys happen a few doors away, close enough to hear the glass. Albert walks out of Chicago that night and is not seen for six weeks; he will come back of his own accord, into the courtroom, to stand with the men who were arrested. Lucy stays in the city with two children and a shop, and is picked up and released so often over the next six months that nobody keeps a tally.
suggested_refs: Zepf's Hall, Lake and Desplaines, adjoining Haymarket Square
sources: IWW archive, 'Lucy Parsons: Woman of Will'

stops.name: The Arbeiter-Zeitung office, arrested without a warrant
stops.date_confidence: The warrantless raid on the Arbeiter-Zeitung office, Parsons's arrest and release without charge, and the officer's slur are attested [A] by Wikipedia. The coordinate is 107 Fifth Avenue (later North Wells Street); the address is the standard one in the Haymarket literature but is not printed in the Wikipedia entries consulted, so the pin carries moderate confidence. The lens's original 41.8853,-87.632 lay roughly 200 m NE.
stops.campa: The police come into the offices of the Arbeiter-Zeitung on Fifth Avenue without a warrant, take the presses apart, and arrest everyone in the building including Lucy Parsons. An officer calls her a black bitch. It is on the record, and she never in her life answers it by claiming the word did not apply to her. Over the following weeks the city arrests hundreds of people without warrants and no court in Illinois stops it. She is let go without a charge.
suggested_refs: The Chicagoer Arbeiter-Zeitung, edited by August Spies, at 107 Fifth Avenue
sources: IWW archive, 'Lucy Parsons: Woman of Will'

stops.name: Cook County Criminal Court, the indictment and the verdict
stops.date_confidence: The grand jury indictment of 31 men on 27 May 1886, Parsons's and Holmes's non-indictment, the trial from June to August, the verdict of 20 August 1886 and the death sentences on seven defendants are attested [A]. Parsons's attendance at every day of the trial is [A] per Wikipedia. The coordinate is corrected to the Cook County Criminal Court Building on Hubbard Street at Dearborn, per Wikipedia's Cook County Jail entry; the lens's original 41.8869,-87.6313 lay roughly 350 m south and contradicted its own jail coordinate on the same block.
stops.campa: A grand jury indicts thirty-one men. Lucy Parsons, who has told the unemployed of Chicago in print to learn the use of explosives, is not among them; neither is Lizzie Holmes. The prosecution never claims that any defendant threw the bomb. Eight men are tried on the theory that their words made them accessories, and the whole of the defence budget is what Lucy can raise from a dress shop. On the twentieth of August seven are sentenced to hang. She is in the courtroom every day of it, and the reporters describe her clothes.
stops.quote: Let the masses understand that these robbers hold this property (which is so much unpaid labor) under the plea of the laws which they themselves have made
stops.quote_source: Lucy Parsons, quoted in Keith Rosenthal, 'Lucy Parsons: More Dangerous Than a Thousand Rioters' (The Anarchist Library); undated, not spoken at the trial
suggested_refs: The Cook County Criminal Court Building, Hubbard and Dearborn, Chicago
Trial transcript, Illinois v. August Spies et al. (1886), Chicago Historical Society
sources: Grunge.com, 'The Untold History of Lucy and Albert Parsons'

segments.name: Seven Weeks, and the Eleventh of November

stops.name: Cincinnati, the tour begins
stops.date_confidence: The seven-week tour, the circuit through Cincinnati, New York, Philadelphia, New Haven and Columbus, and the estimate of some 200,000 people addressed are attested [A] by Wikipedia and the IWW archive biography. The two lenses date the tour differently: the chronology places it in 1886, between conviction and execution, while the geography lens gives 1887-1888. The 1886-1887 window is used here because it fits the stated purpose of raising funds for the condemned. Day unknown, defaulted to 01. The meeting at Sheffield, Indiana, held just outside Chicago police jurisdiction, is [R] from the IWW archive biography and is named in the campa rather than given its own stop.
stops.campa: Between the verdict and the executions she goes out on the road for seven weeks and speaks, by her own count and the movement's, to something near two hundred thousand people: Cincinnati first, then New York, Philadelphia, New Haven, Columbus. She is raising money for the appeal and for seven families. There is also a meeting at Sheffield, Indiana, held just outside the reach of the Chicago police. Whether the seven weeks moved anything in Illinois, nobody has ever been able to say.
suggested_refs: The Amnesty Association and the defence fund for the Haymarket condemned
sources: IWW archive, 'Lucy Parsons: Woman of Will'

stops.name: New Haven, the tour's most quoted hour
stops.date_confidence: New Haven as a tour stop is attested [A] by the IWW archive biography, which also reports her most quoted line of the tour there; the exact wording of that line is not reproduced in any source reachable this session, so no quote is carried here. Month and day unknown, defaulted to 01-01. That she sold pamphlets at the door to fund the next ticket is [R], from the general account of the tour's finances.
stops.campa: In New Haven she gives the tour its most quoted hour. She is not asking for sympathy and says so; she is asking whether a country that will not hear a petition can be made to hear something else. The halls are full and the local papers are hostile. She is crossing New England alone in winter with a satchel of pamphlets, selling them at the door to pay for the next ticket. What she actually said in New Haven, the line everyone afterward agreed was the best of the tour, nobody wrote down.
stops.quote: they have never yet deigned to notice any petition from their slaves that they were not compelled to read by the red glare bursting from the cannon's mouths
stops.quote_source: Lucy Parsons, 'To Tramps' (1884), text via libcom.org and The Anarchist Library
suggested_refs: Lucy Parsons's 1886-1887 lecture circuit through the Northeast
sources: IWW archive, 'Lucy Parsons: Woman of Will'

stops.name: Franklin County Jail, Columbus
stops.date_confidence: Being prevented from speaking in Columbus and briefly jailed in Franklin County is attested [A] by Wikipedia and the IWW archive biography, undated within the tour. Month and day chosen only to order the segment. Governor Oglesby's commutation of the Fielden and Schwab sentences and Louis Lingg's suicide, both on 10 November 1887, are attested [A].
stops.campa: Columbus will not let her speak. The police stop the meeting and put her in the Franklin County jail, briefly, on no charge that survives the night. The same thing will be done to her in a dozen cities over the next fifty years: a hall hired, a crowd assembled, an officer at the door. She goes on to the next city. The tour finishes and the sentences stand. In November Governor Oglesby commutes two of them, and Louis Lingg kills himself in his cell with a smuggled cap of dynamite the day before the rest are to hang.
suggested_refs: Governor Richard J. Oglesby's commutation order of 10 November 1887
sources: IWW archive, 'Lucy Parsons: Woman of Will'

stops.name: Chicago Avenue station, stripped and held until three
stops.date_confidence: Corrected date. Wikipedia places the attempted final visit, the strip search for explosives and the detention until 15:00 on 11 November 1887, the execution day itself, with Lizzie Holmes accompanying her, not on the eve as one research entry had it. The coordinate is corrected to the East Chicago Avenue station at 113 West Chicago Avenue; the lens's original 41.8963,-87.6371 lay roughly 550 m west. That she was not allowed to see the body until the following day is [R].
stops.campa: On the morning of the eleventh she takes Albert Junior, eight, and Lulu, six, to the jail to see their father, with Lizzie Holmes beside her. The police arrest all of them at the door, take the two women to the Chicago Avenue station, strip them naked to search for explosives, and hold them in a cell until three in the afternoon. By three the men are dead. She is not allowed to see the body until the next day, and the children never see him at all. Albert's last words from the trap, which she does not hear, are a request to be allowed to speak.
suggested_refs: The East Chicago Avenue police station, 113 W Chicago Avenue
sources: IWW archive, 'Lucy Parsons: Woman of Will'

stops.name: Cook County Jail, the hanging
stops.date_confidence: Attested [A]: Albert Parsons hanged with August Spies, George Engel and Adolph Fischer at the Cook County Jail on 11 November 1887, and over 10,000 people paying respects at Lucy's shop in the days following. One later source (AAIHS, 'Searching for Lucy Parsons: A Racial Riddle') misplaces the execution at Joliet State Prison; the Cook County Jail is the far better attested site and the contradiction is recorded rather than resolved.
stops.campa: Albert Parsons is hanged with August Spies, George Engel and Adolph Fischer in the corridor of the Cook County Jail at Hubbard and Dearborn. They are hooded in white shrouds and the drop is short. In the days that follow more than ten thousand people file through Lucy's shop on Mohawk Street to look at the coffin and to take her hand. She is thirty-six and a widow. The shop stays open through the week of the funeral, the sewing being the only income in the house.
suggested_refs: The Cook County Jail, attached to the Criminal Court Building at Hubbard and Dearborn
sources: Chicago History Museum, 'Lucy Parsons: A Fighter for Workers' Rights'

stops.name: German Waldheim, the procession
stops.date_confidence: Attested [A]: a funeral procession of 10,000 to 15,000 on 13 November 1887, with Lucy walking behind the casket, ending at German Waldheim (now Forest Home) Cemetery in Forest Park. The ban on red flags and banners on the route is [R], standard in the Haymarket literature. The two research lenses gave different coordinates for the same cemetery (41.8703,-87.8241 and 41.86972,-87.81972); the first is used consistently here and the discrepancy is left flagged.
stops.campa: Between ten and fifteen thousand people walk out to German Waldheim behind the caskets, with brass bands and the Marseillaise, and the city permits no red flags and no banners on the route. Lucy walks behind her husband's coffin the whole distance. The cemetery is outside the city limits, which is the reason the graves are there: no Chicago ground would take them. She will be buried in the same plot fifty-five years later, and she will spend a good part of the interval raising the money for the monument that stands over it.
suggested_refs: Forest Home Cemetery (German Waldheim), Forest Park, Illinois
sources: IWW archive, 'Lucy Parsons: Woman of Will'

stops.name: The Socialist League, London: six weeks of platforms
stops.date_confidence: Arrival in London in October 1888, the six-week tour, addressing the Socialist League, sharing platforms with William Morris and Peter Kropotkin, and the public disagreement with Annie Besant over violence are attested [A] by Wikipedia and by Lichtenstein, 'Lucy Parsons's Propaganda Tour of Britain', History (2025). The timing against the first anniversaries of the hangings and of Bloody Sunday is [R]. The precise date is chosen only to order the segment; the coordinate is a central London placeholder for a tour of many halls.
stops.campa: She lands in England in October and the Socialist League puts her on platform after platform across London for six weeks. She shares them with Peter Kropotkin and argues in public with Annie Besant, who will not accept the Chicago defence of violence. Parsons does not soften it for an English audience. The first anniversary of the hangings falls during the tour, and so does the first anniversary of Bloody Sunday in Trafalgar Square. Whether the League planned the dates that way is not recorded.

stops.name: Kelmscott House, Hammersmith, the Upper Mall
stops.date_confidence: That Parsons spoke at William Morris's home during the British tour is attested [A] by Lichtenstein and the Black Outdoors blog. The specific date of 15 November 1888 could not be verified in any source reachable this session: Wikipedia dates only the October arrival, and the date is retained here solely on the Lichtenstein citation supplied by the research pool. The coordinate is the canonical Kelmscott House pin already used in william_morris.journey.json, inherited byte-identical.
stops.campa: On the Upper Mall at Hammersmith, in the coach house beside William Morris's river-facing home, Lucy Parsons addresses the Hammersmith branch of the Socialist League. Morris is fifty-four and about to begin News from Nowhere; Parsons is a Chicago seamstress who buried her husband ten months ago. The room holds a couple of hundred. What the designer of wallpapers and the widow of a hanged printer had to say to one another is not recorded, and both of them left a great deal on paper.

stops.name: The Tower of London, with Jane Morris
stops.date_confidence: Attested [A]: Wikipedia's Lucy Parsons entry records that she visited the Tower of London and Westminster Abbey with Jane Morris, upgrading a research entry that had tagged both as [R] tourist notes. The exact dates within the tour are not given; the date here orders the segment only. Coordinate is the Tower of London.
stops.campa: Jane Morris takes her to see the Tower of London and then Westminster Abbey. It is the only tourism in six weeks of halls and trains: the woman who sat for Rossetti as Proserpine and Astarte Syriaca, walking an American anarchist through the armouries and the royal tombs. A year earlier the state of Illinois had hanged her husband. Parsons leaves no account of what she made of the Tower, and Jane Morris left none either. She is back on a platform the same week.
suggested_refs: Westminster Abbey, visited on the same outing
sources: IWW archive, 'Lucy Parsons: Woman of Will'

stops.name: The Port of New York, the return
stops.date_confidence: Return by ship to New York in December 1888 is attested [A] by the IWW archive biography; the exact date and vessel are not given, and the day here orders the segment only. The characterization of her subsequent income is [R].
stops.campa: She lands in New York in December with the tour behind her and no husband to come home to. The English weeks have given her a reputation on two continents and no income. From here it is the train back to Chicago, the shop, the two children, and the work she will do without interruption for the next fifty-four years: writing, editing, speaking on street corners when the halls are closed to her, and being arrested for it. She is thirty-seven years old and has fifty-four years to live.

stops.name: Chicago, the Life of Albert R. Parsons and the lecture the chief forbade
stops.date_confidence: The 1889 self-published Life of Albert R. Parsons, the allegation that Martin Lacher wrote much of it, Chief George W. Hubbard's suppression of her lecture 'Review of the Labor Movement in Europe' and Lacher's arrest are all attested [A] by Wikipedia. The expanded second edition of 1903 is [A] per Open Library and bookseller listings. Her editorship of Freedom is dated 1891 by Wikipedia and 1890-1892 by the Texas State Historical Association; the discrepancy is left standing. Month and day unknown, defaulted to 01-01.
stops.campa: She writes and publishes the Life of Albert R. Parsons herself, a biography and a brief for the dead, and sells it out of the shop; some accounts hold that her younger companion Martin Lacher wrote much of the text. The same year Chief George Hubbard forbids her to deliver a lecture on the European labour movement, and Lacher is arrested for protesting the ban. From about 1890 she edits Freedom, an anarchist-communist paper, and prints in it what the daily press will not carry about lynching and about convict labour.

stops.name: Mohawk Street, Lulu Eda
stops.date_confidence: Corrected date. Wikipedia gives Lulu Eda Parsons born 20 April 1881 and dead of lymphedema at the age of eight, which places the death between April 1889 and April 1890, not 1888 as one research entry had it; the 'seven or eight' hedge in another entry is dropped in favour of age eight. Month and day chosen only to order the segment. That Lucy left no written record of the death is an argument from silence and is stated as such.
stops.campa: Lulu Eda Parsons dies of lymphedema at eight years old. She was born in April 1881; she is the child who was carried to the jail door on the morning of the executions and turned back by the police without seeing her father. At the time of the death her mother is editing Freedom and keeping the shop on Mohawk Street. Nothing survives of what Lucy Parsons said or did in the weeks afterward, in her own papers or in anyone else's. Albert Junior, born in 1879, is the surviving child.

stops.name: Newark, arrested on the street
stops.date_confidence: Attested [A] by Wikipedia and the IWW archive biography: prevented from speaking in Newark in November 1890 and arrested in the street on a charge of incitement to riot. Day unknown, defaulted to 01. The Chicago Police Department's description of her as 'more dangerous than a thousand rioters' is widely cited [A as a quotation in circulation] but no source reachable this session names the officer, the document or the date; the ZNetwork and SocialistWorker accounts attach it loosely to the 1920s-1930s Red Squad, so its placement in 1890 here is an ordering device, not a dating claim.
stops.campa: Newark will not let her speak either. The police break up the meeting and arrest her in the street on a charge of incitement to riot, and the charge does what such charges are for, which is to cost her the hall, the fare and the evening. By now the pattern is settled across a dozen states: she is permitted to publish, more or less, and forbidden to be heard aloud. Somewhere in the Chicago police department someone writes down a working description of her: more dangerous than a thousand rioters. No one has ever found the document.
stops.quote: more dangerous than a thousand rioters
stops.quote_source: Chicago Police Department description of Lucy Parsons, widely cited (Keith Rosenthal, The Anarchist Library; SocialistWorker.org); no original document identified

stops.name: Avondale, the house at 999 Hammond Avenue and the fire of 1896
stops.date_confidence: The Avondale house at 999 Hammond Avenue (later North Troy Street), the August 1896 fire, the damage to her book stock and her selling the fire-damaged copies afterward are attested [A] by Wikipedia and the IWW archive biography. Day unknown, defaulted to 01. The library figure of roughly 3,000 volumes is attested for the end of her life, not for 1896.
stops.campa: She builds a house at 999 Hammond Avenue in Avondale, on the north-west edge of the city, and fills it with books: several thousand of them by the end, on socialism, on anarchy, on sex, most of them bought secondhand out of a seamstress's earnings. In August a fire runs through it and scorches her stock of pamphlets. She sells them afterward as fire-damaged copies at a reduced price, because she needs the money and because the stock is what she has. The street is renamed North Troy. She will die in this house.
suggested_refs: 999 Hammond Avenue, later North Troy Street, Avondale, Chicago
sources: IWW archive, 'Lucy Parsons: Woman of Will'

stops.name: Chicago, the quarrel with Emma Goldman
stops.date_confidence: The 1897 meeting through the Social Democracy of America is attested [A] by Wikipedia. The substance of the clash is corrected here: Goldman advocated free love against Parsons's defence of monogamy, where one research entry had attributed both positions to Goldman. Goldman's later coolness toward Parsons and its reading are [R]. Month and day unknown, defaulted to 01-01; coordinate is the canonical Chicago pin, no meeting place being named.
stops.campa: Emma Goldman is twenty-eight when they meet through the Social Democracy of America. Parsons is forty-six and has been on Chicago platforms since before Goldman landed in the country. They do not get on. Goldman preaches free love; Parsons defends monogamy and says the economic question comes first and everything else after it. Goldman will later write about Parsons with a coolness that has been read as jealousy and as something less flattering than jealousy. She never says outright what she meant by it.
suggested_refs: Emma Goldman, Living My Life (1931), on Lucy Parsons

stops.name: Elgin, the son committed
stops.date_confidence: Corrected agency and end date. Wikipedia: after Albert Jr. attempted to enlist, Lucy Parsons herself had him committed to the Northern Illinois State Mental Hospital in 1899, and he remained there until his death from tuberculosis in 1919. A research entry had left the committal agentless. Month and day unknown, defaulted to 01-01. Her reasons are not recorded anywhere reachable and are stated here as a gap. Coordinate is Elgin, Illinois.
stops.campa: Albert Parsons Junior, twenty, tries to enlist for the war in Cuba: to fight for the government that hanged his father. His mother has him committed to the Northern Illinois State Hospital at Elgin instead. He stays there twenty years and dies of tuberculosis in 1919 without coming out. What she thought she was doing, and whether the enlistment or something else was the reason, she never wrote down and nobody who knew her recorded asking. His ashes are put into her grave later, by other hands.
suggested_refs: Northern Illinois State Hospital (Elgin State Hospital), Elgin, Illinois

stops.name: Chicago, the press of Free Society broken
stops.date_confidence: Corrected date. Wikipedia: 'By 1900, Parsons was the Chicago correspondent for Free Society which had its printing press destroyed by the police following the assassination of President William McKinley.' McKinley was shot on 6 September and died on 14 September 1901, so the press destruction belongs to 1901 and only the correspondent role is 'by 1900'; a research entry had collapsed both into 1900. The Anarchist Exclusion Act of 1903 is [A]. Coordinate is the anarchist press district around Fifth Avenue, a placeholder: no address for the Free Society office was found this session.
stops.campa: By 1900 she is the Chicago correspondent of Free Society. In September of the following year Leon Czolgosz shoots President McKinley in Buffalo and says an anarchist lecture put it in his head, and the country's police go through the anarchist press like a threshing machine. The Free Society press is destroyed. Congress will shortly pass an act barring anarchists from entering the United States. Parsons, who cannot be deported because she was born inside it, goes on printing.

stops.name: Brand's Hall, the founding of the IWW
stops.date_confidence: Attested [A]: 200 delegates at Brand's Hall on 27 June 1905, with Debs, Mother Jones and Lucy Parsons among the speakers (Wikipedia, 'Big Bill Haywood'); libcom confirms the 'slaves of slaves' passage and that Parsons addressed the convention on two occasions. Two research entries claimed she was the only woman among the founders or the only woman to address the convention; both are false, since Mother Jones is named in the same sources, and are corrected here to one of two women. She also edited The Liberator in 1905 [A, Texas State Historical Association]. Coordinate corrected to the near North Side, Clark at Erie; the lens's 41.8977,-87.6533 lay roughly 1.8 km west.
stops.campa: Two hundred delegates fill Brand's Hall on Clark Street in June for what William Haywood opens by calling the Continental Congress of the working class. Eugene Debs is there, and Mother Jones, and Lucy Parsons, one of only two women among the convention's prominent speakers, who addresses it twice. She speaks about the women in the sweatshops and about the strike that does not walk out but stays in and takes the machinery. She is fifty-four and has been doing this for twenty-eight years. That autumn she edits The Liberator.
stops.quote: We are the slaves of slaves. We are exploited more ruthlessly than men.
stops.quote_source: Lucy Parsons, address to the founding convention of the Industrial Workers of the World, Brand's Hall, Chicago, 27 June 1905 (libcom.org; 1905 IWW convention minutes)

stops.name: Avondale, the Syndicalist League in her front room
stops.date_confidence: Attested [A] by Wikipedia: Parsons hosted the meeting establishing the Syndicalist League of North America in 1912, with William Z. Foster staying at her home at the time. The coordinate is corrected to her Avondale house: a research entry gave a generic Loop point that contradicted its own claim text and was reused for three unrelated stops. Month and day unknown, defaulted to 01-01. The League's size and equipment are [R].
stops.campa: William Z. Foster comes back from France full of syndicalism, stays in Lucy Parsons's Avondale house, and the founding meeting of the Syndicalist League of North America is held in her front room. She is sixty-one. Foster will end as chairman of the Communist Party; Parsons will end in it too, though not for another twenty-seven years and not by his road. For the moment the League is a handful of people and a mimeograph, in a house full of books, on the north-west side of Chicago.

stops.name: Halsted Street, the hunger march past Hull House
stops.date_confidence: Attested [A] by Wikipedia and the IWW archive biography: arrested in January 1915 with Father Irwin St John Tucker and nineteen others after speaking at a hunger march of roughly 1,500 unemployed on Halsted Street near Hull House. The day within January is not given in the sources and is chosen only to order the segment. The count of her arrests to that date is [R] and is stated as a minimum.
stops.campa: Fifteen hundred unemployed march on Halsted Street in the depression winter, past Hull House, and Lucy Parsons speaks to them. The police arrest her along with Irwin St John Tucker, an Episcopal priest, and nineteen others. The charge is the usual one and it goes nowhere, as usual. She has been speaking on Chicago streets for thirty-eight years by this date. It is at minimum her twelfth arrest, and the count is a minimum because nobody, including her, kept a full list.

stops.name: The Ashland Auditorium, May Day at seventy-nine
stops.date_confidence: Attested [A] by Wikipedia and the IWW archive biography: a May Day speech to thousands at the Ashland Auditorium in 1930, later reprinted in United States Congressional hearings investigating communist activities. That the reprinting is how much of her late oratory survives is [R], an inference from the state of the record.
stops.campa: On May Day she fills the Ashland Auditorium: an old woman on a platform in front of thousands, at an age when most of the men who were arrested with her at Haymarket have been dead for forty years. A stenographer takes the speech down for the government. It is reprinted afterward in the record of a Congressional inquiry into communist activity, which is how a good deal of what she said in these years survives at all, filed by the people who were watching her. She is seventy-nine.
stops.quote: My conception of the strike of the future is not to strike and go out and starve, but to strike and remain in and take possession of the necessary property of production
stops.quote_source: Lucy Parsons, speech, quoted in Keith Rosenthal, 'Lucy Parsons: More Dangerous Than a Thousand Rioters' (The Anarchist Library)

stops.name: Avondale, joining the Communist Party at eighty-eight
stops.date_confidence: Attested [A] by Wikipedia: blind, living in poverty in Avondale with a personal library of roughly 3,000 books, Parsons formally joined the Communist Party USA in 1939. Month and day unknown, defaulted to 01-01. Her reasons are not on record; the reading offered here is [R], inferred from her decade of prior work with Communist-led defence campaigns, which is itself [A].
stops.campa: She is blind now, or close to it, poor, living on very little in the Avondale house with the books she can no longer read, and in 1939 she joins the Communist Party of the United States. Anarchists have called it a surrender ever since. She had been working alongside Communist-led defence campaigns for a decade before she signed anything. The Party still had an office, a lawyer and a press. Why she signed she did not write down, and nobody who visited her that year appears to have asked.
stops.quote: the struggle for liberty is too great and the few steps we have gained have been at too great a sacrifice, for the great mass of the people ... to consent to turn over to any political party the management of our social and industrial affairs
stops.quote_source: Lucy Parsons, quoted in Keith Rosenthal, 'Lucy Parsons: More Dangerous Than a Thousand Rioters' (The Anarchist Library); written decades before she joined the CPUSA

stops.name: Chicago, the last May Day
stops.date_confidence: Attested [A] by Wikipedia and the IWW archive biography: her last public appearance, as guest of honour at a May Day event with the Farm Equipment Workers' Organizing Committee, on 1 May 1941. No venue is named in any source reachable this session, so the canonical Chicago pin is used. That nothing she said was recorded is an argument from silence and is stated as such.
stops.campa: It is fifty-five years to the month since the eighty thousand came down Michigan Avenue. Her last appearance in public is at a May Day event, as guest of honour of the Farm Equipment Workers' Organizing Committee: a union of men building tractors, seating a blind woman of ninety at the head table because her husband was hanged in this city for demanding the eight-hour day they now work. She speaks. Nobody wrote down what she said, and nothing of it survives in the labour press or anywhere else.

stops.name: Avondale, the fire and the carts of books
stops.date_confidence: Death by house fire on 7 March 1942 at an age given variously as 89 or 91, and George Markstall's death of his injuries the following day, are attested [A]. The cause of the fire is disputed: Ashbaugh gives a wood stove, another account a basement water heater. The library's fate is deliberately split: police seizure of the books and papers from the gutted house is [A] per libcom, while FBI custody is [R] and contested, reaching us secondhand through Ben Reitman being told so by the head of the Chicago Red Squad, and the FBI itself denied any knowledge of the books. Part of the library burned rather than being taken. The coordinate is the Avondale house; one research lens had wrongly placed the death at the Loop pin.
stops.campa: Fire takes the Avondale house on a night in March. George Markstall, her companion of many years, gets out and goes back in for her and cannot bring her out; he dies of his burns the next day. She is about ninety-one. A wood stove is blamed in one account and a basement water heater in another. The police go through the wet ruins afterward and carry away what the fire left of the three thousand books and all of her papers. None of it is ever returned, catalogued or seen again. Asked about the books, the FBI says it has never heard of them.
suggested_refs: Carolyn Ashbaugh, Lucy Parsons: American Revolutionary (1976)
Ben Reitman's account of the Chicago Red Squad and the seized library

stops.name: Forest Home Cemetery, beside the monument she paid for
stops.date_confidence: Attested [A]: a memorial service attended by roughly 300 people and burial at German Waldheim (now Forest Home) Cemetery, Forest Park, near the Haymarket Martyrs' Monument, on 12 March 1942; the later interment of the ashes of Albert Jr. and George Markstall in her grave is [A] per the Forest Home Cemetery Overview. The Haymarket Martyrs' Monument by Albert Weinert was dedicated on 25 June 1893 [A]. The two research lenses gave conflicting coordinates for the cemetery (41.8703,-87.8241 and 41.86972,-87.81972); the first is used throughout this file and the discrepancy is left flagged rather than resolved.
stops.campa: Three hundred people come to the memorial. She is buried at German Waldheim, now Forest Home, a few yards from the Haymarket Martyrs' Monument she spent years raising the money to put up, and beside Albert Parsons, dead fifty-four years. The ashes of her son and of George Markstall go into the same grave afterward. The stone over the martyrs carries August Spies's last words from the trap. She had spent fifty-four years insisting the men under it were right.
